title: Clovis people didn't just hunt mammoths — they painted and sewed inside tents
dek: Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles turned up at the LaPrele site in Wyoming, and DNA protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the "mammoth hunter" label suggests.
why: High density of archaeological detail, but it demands patience: the first half is Clovis research history and dating debates, and the concrete findings at LaPrele in the second half are the part that's really worth your time.
who: Readers interested in American prehistoric archaeology, Ice Age human adaptation strategies, or hunter-gatherer spatial organization; also suited to engineers following new archaeological techniques like ZooMS.
skip: The host's introduction in the first 2 minutes and the two History Hit ads in the middle can be skipped.

points.h: Clovis lasted only a few hundred years
points.body: Radiocarbon dating pins Clovis culture to roughly 13,100 to 12,750 years ago, a window of a few hundred years just before the end of the Ice Age. The narrowness of that span is itself startling — the Ice Age runs on scales of tens to hundreds of thousands of years, and Clovis is a single instant within it. More crucially, within those few hundred years, highly similar fluted stone spear points appeared across the entire North American continent, from New Mexico to Wyoming and from Washington State to Virginia. That combination of narrow time and wide space is Clovis's most distinctive feature; in later periods, spear points rapidly regionalized.

points.h: Clovis was not the first Americans
points.body: The "Clovis First" theory dominated most of the 20th century: humans followed mammoth herds into the Americas, and Clovis people were the earliest settlers. But finds at Monte Verde (Chile), Paisley Caves (Oregon), Cooper's Ferry (Idaho) and Page-Ladson (Florida) have led most archaeologists to now believe people were living in the Americas thousands of years before Clovis. Mackey says this is one of the fiercest debates in American archaeology, and Pleistocene archaeologists argue about it hard. But she also stresses that Clovis research shouldn't fixate only on the question of "who came first" — there are many questions worth asking about their lives themselves.

points.h: One chopper changed the nature of the whole site
points.body: The LaPrele site was found in 1986 when locals spotted mammoth bones by a creek, and Mackey and collaborators returned to excavate in the 2000s. In the first season, retired archaeologist Rich Adams, helping everyone fix the screening channel, found a large chopper about 10 meters from the mammoth — a simple tool made by knocking a few flakes off a river cobble. The key is that it appeared in a position where it geologically shouldn't: the site was gradually buried by floods, and natural processes were unlikely to have moved such a large cobble there. That tool pushed the team to test on a larger scale, eventually uncovering more than 50,000 flakes, at least four artifact concentration areas, several hundred stone tools and mammoth ivory. LaPrele was no longer just a kill site but a camp where humans had lived.

points.h: Hearths and tent walls left fingerprints in the sediment
points.body: LaPrele's most striking find is four "hearth-centered areas." In Block B, the team found no obvious ash or oxidized traces, but burned bone and flakes concentrated in a small patch, indicating a hearth once stood there. Even better is the spatial analysis: if you look down at a tent from above, the hearth is at the center, activity-dense areas surround it, then an open space for walking, and near the tent wall objects pile up — because the wall is a barrier to artifact movement. Block B's artifact distribution shows exactly this "bullseye" pattern, indicating an interior space. In the same area they also found a roughly 1.5-by-2-meter scatter of ochre (hematite) pigment matching the wall's position, suggesting people painted by the fire.

points.h: The bone needles were made from red fox and felid bone
points.body: The team used ZooMS (Zooarchaeology by Mass Spectrometry) to analyze bone needles and possible bone beads; the method extracts proteins from extremely small bone samples to identify the animal species. The results were unexpected: many needles were made from hare bone, but one was red fox and another tested as felid — not a domestic cat, but some wild felid. Mackey notes these are all fur-bearing animals, and their bone thickness may have been just right for needles. More importantly, these animals were probably caught in traps rather than hunted with spears. That means Clovis people weren't hunting mammoths 24 hours a day; they were also taking more common small prey.

points.h: Were Clovis people mammoth specialists or omnivores
points.body: About 15 widely accepted Clovis sites in North America are associated with megafauna, mostly proboscideans (mammoth, mastodon, gomphothere), plus horse and camel. But Mackey points out that only about 30 to 40 sites truly define our understanding of Clovis, while thousands of Clovis spear points have been found on the surface, lacking context. That raises a core debate: were they mammoth-hunting specialists, or omnivores with a broader diet? Small animals, fish and plant remains preserve less well and are less often systematically sought. Mackey is studying plant remains, and she notes archaeologists usually look for plants only in hearths, and how many places in the Clovis record have actually been looked at is itself a problem.

points.h: Mammoth extinction: did humans push, or was climate the main driver
points.body: The classic "overkill" debate: 35 genera of megafauna went extinct at the end of the Ice Age, and how much was human versus environmental? Mackey says she takes a middle path, believing both contributed. She considers mammoths the strongest candidate for the overkill hypothesis, because mammoth sites are numerous, the animals were large and had low reproductive rates, making them more vulnerable to hunting. But she also notes overkill doesn't necessarily mean humans hunted all 35 genera; hunting may have upset the balance through trophic cascades. Interestingly, paleoecologists lean toward "humans did it," while archaeologists lean more toward "the environment did it."

Apart from a single case of ancestral remains attributed to Clovis at the Anzick site in Montana, we have almost no Clovis human bone. Mackey doesn't find this surprising: population density was extremely low, 13,000-year-old sites are inherently extremely hard to preserve, and these groups were highly mobile, so we don't know their burial practices. She also stresses that Clovis people are the ancestors of millions of Indigenous people in the Americas today, and any related research must proceed on the basis of consultation and collaboration.

The distinctive technique of knocking flakes off the center of a spear point's base to form a groove.
Zooarchaeology by Mass Spectrometry, a technique that identifies animal species by analyzing bone collagen proteins, needing only a tiny sample.
Hematite, a red pigment often used in prehistoric painting and decoration.
Human activity areas centered on a hearth, reflecting a camp's spatial organization.
The academic debate over whether human hunting caused the extinction of Ice Age megafauna.

quotes.text: That is, I think, most people, when they think of Clovis, what they think of is that, like, iconic image of a small group of humans kind of stalking this giant, multi-ton animal.
Instead of dragging portions of that animal back to your house, it makes much more sense to just move your house to that animal.
And then when you get near a wall of a tent, you know, that's your storage spot. Right. Or that's a spot where you can't sit yourself. The wall's too close and things kind of accrue there.
So that is revealing that Clovis peoples, they're not just hunting mammoths 24-7, not just the big beasts.
You can be a megafauna specialist and still eat a fish.
